title: Comparison of Urinary Red Blood Cell Distribution (URD) and Dysmorphic Red Blood Cells for Detecting Glomerular Hematuria: A Multicenter Study
condition_or_topic: Differentiating glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria using urinary red blood cell distribution (URD) and dysmorphic red blood cells (dRBC).
clinical_background: Urinary RBC morphology can help identify the source of hematuria, but microscopic recognition of dRBC depends on observer expertise and may vary between laboratories. URD measures the fraction of small RBCs among non-lysed RBCs with an automated analyzer, offering a potentially more objective measure. Earlier studies were largely conducted at single centers and reported variable thresholds for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria, leaving the clinical utility of URD uncertain.
objectives: Compare the diagnostic performance, measured values and cutoff values of URD and dRBC across participating institutions, and assess their clinical significance for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria.
Examine associations between URD and renal parameters, including specific gravity.
Investigate cases in which URD and dRBC results disagree.
clinical_question: In patients with hematuria evaluated at participating medical centers (Patient), how does automated URD measurement (Index test), compared with microscopic dRBC assessment (Comparator), perform in distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria (Outcome)?
interpretation: URD and dRBC distinguished glomerular from extrarenal disease with comparable overall AUC values (0.827 and 0.792, respectively; p = 0.197). URD had higher reported sensitivity and specificity and was less dependent on observer interpretation. Both measures were elevated in glomerular disease and NS, whereas URD was significantly lower in AKI. URD correlated with dRBC and ACR, but not with SG. Discordant results indicate that the measures capture different RBC characteristics: normally sized dRBC can yield a low URD, while small isomorphic RBC or yeasts can yield a high URD.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors describe their findings as consistent with earlier reports of more small RBCs in GH than in NGH. Charoensappakit reported an AUC of 0.9 for %Total PS-RBCs + RMPs, but the authors note that the method was costly and could not measure routine urinalysis parameters. Compared with the single-center studies by Mizuno and Cho using UF-5000, this study included more participants (703 versus 203 and 263) and reported a higher URD AUC (0.827 versus 0.649 and 0.814). Mizuno reported a dRBC–URD correlation of 0.465, compared with 0.536 here. Earlier studies reported widely varying clinically significant dRBC cutoffs, from 10% to 90%; a separate study associated > 25% dRBC with high specificity and positive predictive value for glomerular disease or GH.
clinical_implications: Because its diagnostic performance was comparable to dRBC and its results were more readily standardized, URD may have wider applicability in distinguishing GH from NGH and in ruling out non-glomerular causes of hematuria.
URD and dRBC are not interchangeable measures of RBC morphology; small isomorphic RBC, normally sized dRBC and yeasts may contribute to discordant classifications.
practice_implications: The authors present instrument-measured URD as a more objective and readily obtainable parameter for differentiating GH from NGH.
The authors state that continuing education in RBC morphology is essential for laboratory personnel who identify dRBC in urine sediment.
limitations: dRBC results varied between institutions despite shared assessment guidelines; ambiguous dRBC morphology prevented consensus in some cases.
More than half of the cases came from institution K. The authors believe this imbalance did not affect the main AUC comparison or the absence of a URD–SG correlation.
strengths: The multicenter study compared serum and urine parameters collected at four hospitals.
Relative to the cited Mizuno and Cho studies, it included more participants and reported individual diagnoses within the glomerular, renal and extrarenal groups.
The study also examined URD and dRBC across renal disease groups and investigated samples with discordant results.
study_design: Multicenter comparison of URD and dRBC for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria. Patients receiving routine renal function evaluations were enrolled at four tertiary medical centers in Korea between December 2020 and December 2021. Researchers reviewed medical records and assigned diagnoses using kidney biopsy findings or clinical diagnoses.

population.description: The study included 703 patients: 169 with biopsy-confirmed glomerular diseases, 360 with renal diseases, and 174 with extrarenal diseases. The renal disease group comprised chronic kidney disease (N = 194), nephrotic syndrome (N = 88), tubulointerstitial diseases (N = 36), acute kidney injury (N = 32), and other conditions (N = 10). All patients in the glomerular disease group underwent kidney biopsy. Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Guideline was used to define AKI, CKD, and glomerular diseases.
inclusion_criteria: Patients undergoing renal function evaluations during routine clinical care at the participating centers.
Urine samples were selected sequentially for microscopic examination.
exclusion_criteria: Samples with ≤ 5 RBC/HPF under the stated study exclusion criteria; the microscopy procedure separately describes excluding samples with less than 5 RBCs per HPF.
Patients with heart valve prostheses or thrombotic microangiopathy.
population.care_setting: Four tertiary medical centers in Korea, during routine clinical care.

interventions: Laboratory technicians measured the proportion of dRBC in urine sediment by microscopy. Samples of 10 mL were centrifuged at 400 ×g for 5 min; 20 μL of resuspended sediment was examined, with screening at ×100 and counting of 200 RBCs at ×400. Acanthocytes, echinocytes, and their variants were classified as dRBC according to Nagahama et al.; burr cells were excluded. Microscopy occurred within 1 h of specimen receipt, and examiners were blinded to diagnoses.

URD was assessed with the UF-5000 at the four centers as the number of small RBC divided by the number of non-lysed RBCs. The instrument defined small RBC by FSC intensity < 70. Urine particle and chemical analyses were completed within 30 min of specimen receipt.

Fasting blood and random urine specimens were collected. Testing included routine urinalysis, urinary protein, albumin and creatinine measurements, and serum total protein, albumin, Cr and BUN. eGFR was calculated using the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) formula; values exceeding 90 mL/min were replaced with 90 mL/min.
comparators: URD versus the microscopic proportion of dRBC.
Patients with glomerular diseases versus patients with extrarenal diseases for the diagnostic ROC analysis.
Glomerular, renal and extrarenal diagnostic groups for laboratory comparisons; renal disease subgroups were also examined.

primary: Diagnostic performance of URD and dRBC in distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria, assessed by ROC AUC, cutoff value, sensitivity and specificity.
secondary: Agreement and discrepant findings between URD and dRBC at institution D.
Correlations of URD and dRBC with renal and urinary laboratory parameters.
Differences in URD, dRBC and renal parameters across diagnostic groups and participating centers.

statistical_methods: Continuous descriptive data were expressed as medians with interquartile ranges, and categorical data as counts and percentages. Normality was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test. ROC curve analysis estimated AUC, cutoff values, sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing GH from NGH. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test and continuous variables using the Kruskal–Wallis test. Correlations among renal function tests were assessed with the Spearman rank correlation test. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Analyses used R software (version 4.0).

Institution K: 101 patients with glomerular disease and 34 with extrarenal disease were included in the institutional ROC analysis. dRBC AUC 0.913, cutoff 20%, sensitivity/specificity 88.1/76.5%; URD AUC 0.988, cutoff 25.9%, sensitivity/specificity 97.0/97.1%. The AUC comparison had p < 0.001.

Institution P: 29 patients with glomerular disease and 8 with extrarenal disease were included in the institutional ROC analysis. dRBC AUC 0.709, cutoff 5%, sensitivity/specificity 82.8/75.0%; URD AUC 0.789, cutoff 25%, sensitivity/specificity 100/75.0%. The AUC comparison had p = 0.207.

Institution S: 27 patients with glomerular disease and 60 with extrarenal disease were included in the institutional ROC analysis. dRBC AUC 0.905, cutoff 25%, sensitivity/specificity 81.5/95.0%; URD AUC 0.812, cutoff 30.6%, sensitivity/specificity 85.2/83.3%. The AUC comparison had p = 0.008.

narrative_summary:
This multicenter study compared urinary red blood cell distribution (URD) with microscopic dysmorphic red blood cell (dRBC) assessment for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria. It enrolled 703 patients at four tertiary medical centers in Korea, including 169 with biopsy-confirmed glomerular disease, 360 with other renal diseases and 174 with extrarenal diseases. Laboratory staff assessed urinary RBC morphology, while automated particle analysis supplied URD measurements.

Median dRBC and URD values were highest in the glomerular group: 60% and 46.4%, respectively, compared with 5% and 10.0% in the extrarenal group. In the glomerular-versus-extrarenal analysis, the overall dRBC and URD cutoffs were 18% and 31.9%; their AUCs were 0.792 and 0.827, with p = 0.197 for the AUC comparison. URD correlated significantly with dRBC (0.536*) and Albumin/Cr (0.186*), but not with SG (−0.028). Within the renal-disease group, dRBC and URD were significantly elevated in NS, whereas URD was significantly lower in AKI.

At institution D, the two classifications agreed in 112/143 cases (78.3%). Discordant findings involved normally sized dRBC, small isomorphic RBC or yeast. The authors consider URD a more objective, readily standardized alternative with comparable diagnostic discrimination. They note between-institution variation in dRBC assessment and that over half of cases came from institution K.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: The clinical usefulness of urinary red blood cell distribution (URD) has remained limited. This multicenter study compared URD with dysmorphic RBC (dRBC) for identifying glomerular hematuria. It included 703 patients from four tertiary medical centers in Korea: 169 with biopsy-confirmed glomerular diseases, 194 with chronic kidney disease, 88 with nephrotic syndrome (NS), 36 with tubulointerstitial diseases, 32 with acute kidney injury, 10 with other renal diseases, and 174 with extrarenal diseases. The investigators assessed renal measures, urine microscopy, urinalysis, and URD. Median dRBC and URD values were significantly higher in glomerular disease. URD correlated significantly with dRBC (r = 0.536) and albumin creatinine ratio (r = 0.186), but not with specific gravity (r =−0.03). Within renal diseases, both measures were higher in NS. dRBC and URD agreed in 78.3% (112/143) of comparisons, leaving 31 discrepancies. For distinguishing glomerular from extrarenal disease, ROC analysis identified cutoffs of 18% for dRBC and 31.9% for URD; their respective areas under the curve (AUC) were 0.79 and 0.83. The authors conclude that URD has comparable diagnostic performance to dRBC while yielding more objective, standardizable results, potentially improving differentiation of glomerular hematuria (GH) from non-GH.

document_sections.heading: 1 | Introduction
document_sections.content: Hematuria means RBCs are present in urine and may be visible or detectable only microscopically. It is a fundamental manifestation of glomerulonephritis (GN); microscopic assessment of urinary sediment is presented as its most effective detection method. Birch et al. proposed in 1979 that urinary RBC morphology could distinguish glomerular from non-glomerular origins. Passage through glomeruli can damage RBC membranes and produce dysmorphic RBCs (dRBCs). Shichiri et al. reported in 1988 that erythrocytes were smaller in glomerular than in non-glomerular disease, and Hyodo et al. later proposed an RBC size range of 4–6 μm for discriminating the origins. Compared with blood, urine has much less albumin and more urea; this environment increases membrane vulnerability and changes RBC shape. High urea concentrations particularly favor burr-cell formation. Passage across the glomerular basement membrane may produce acanthocytes through membrane injury. RBCs in renal disease are also more susceptible to factors including iron deficiency, osmotic lysis, shape distortion, and vesicle formation. Reliable recognition of urinary dRBCs requires an experienced observer, and observer-dependent interpretation may explain differences between laboratories. The authors consider continuing education in RBC morphology essential and mention deep learning for microscopy as another possible approach. Instrument-measured small-RBC fractions are easier to obtain and less dependent on interpretation, making them potentially more objective and standardized. The fully automated UF-5000 uses fluorescence flow cytometry to classify urine particles and reports morphological RBC information, including non-lysed RBCs, lysed RBCs, large RBCs, small RBCs, and RBC-Info. Its classification uses forward scatter light (FSC), side scatter light (SSC), side fluorescence light (SFL), and depolarized side scattered light (DSS). A small RBC has FSC intensity < 70; a non-lysed RBC has a strong FSC signal and morphological stability indicated by SSC. URD is the small-RBC count divided by the non-lysed-RBC count. Earlier studies investigated possible clinical uses, but most were single-center studies. Reported cutoffs for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria varied from 30.1% to 40.5% for small RBCs and from 0% to 30.0% for dRBCs. The authors therefore considered a multicenter assessment using the same equipment necessary for clinical application. Across four hospitals, they collected urine microscopy findings, urine measures, serum markers, and kidney-function information to compare institutional dRBC and URD measurements and cutoffs and assess their clinical significance.

document_sections.heading: 2 | Methods 2.1 | Subjects and Specimen Collections
document_sections.content: Participants underwent kidney-function evaluation during routine care. Fasting blood and random urine were collected. Between December 2020 and December 2021, four Korean tertiary centers, labeled D, K, P, and S, enrolled 703 patients. Laboratory technicians assessed the dRBC proportion in urine sediment. Medical-record review supplied demographic, clinical, and laboratory information and assigned patients, using biopsy or clinical diagnoses, to glomerular diseases (1), renal diseases (2), or extrarenal diseases (3). All patients classified with glomerular disease had kidney biopsies. Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Guideline criteria defined AKI, CKD, and glomerular diseases; the tubulointerstitial classification followed Beck and Salant. The stated exclusions were samples with ≤ 5 RBC/HPF, inadequate clinical information, heart valve prostheses, or thrombotic microangiopathy. Mixed-type hematuria samples were omitted to differentiate GH from non-GH. Table 1 details the diagnostic classifications and their counts. Each participating center's Institutional Review Board approved the study under CR-21-012-L and waived informed consent.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 | Urine Microscopic Examination
document_sections.content: Urine samples of 10 mL underwent centrifugation at 400 ×g for 5 min. After removal of the supernatant, the sediment was resuspended and 20 μL was taken for examination. Screening used low-power microscopy (×100); dRBC counting used high-power fields (HPF, ×400) and 200 RBCs. RBC counts were grouped as 5–9, 10–29, or ≥ 30. Samples were selected sequentially, with those containing less than 5 RBCs per HPF excluded from this analysis. In accordance with Nagahama et al.'s classification, dRBCs comprised acanthocytes, echinocytes, and their variants; burr cells were excluded. dRBC was calculated as a percentage of all RBCs. Microscopy took place within 1 h of specimen receipt, and examiners did not know the patient's diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 | Urine Parameter Measurement
document_sections.content: Routine urinalysis and urinary protein, albumin, and creatinine measurements were performed. All four tertiary laboratories analyzed urine particles with the fully automated UF-5000. Institution P used AU5800 for the specified chemical measurements, whereas D, K, and S used COBAS C702. Urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) and protein-to-creatinine ratio (PCR) were measured in some patients. Urine-strip testing used UC 3500 at K, P, and S and Uriscan Super+ at D. Particle and chemical urine analyses were completed within 30 min after specimen receipt.

document_sections.heading: 2.4 | Serum Parameter Measurements
document_sections.content: Chemical analyzers measured serum total protein, albumin, creatinine (Cr), and blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Institution P used AU5800; the other three centers used COBAS C702. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated with the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) formula. eGFR results above 90 mL/min were replaced with 90 mL/min.

document_sections.heading: 2.5 | Comparison of dRBC and URD Results for Differential Diagnosis Between Glomerular Hematuria (GH) and Non-glomerular Hematuria (NGH)
document_sections.content: The investigators compared dRBC and URD areas under the curve (AUC) in receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis to assess differentiation of glomerular from extrarenal disease. They examined discordant dRBC and URD findings at hospital D.

document_sections.heading: 2.6 | Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: Continuous descriptive results were expressed as medians and interquartile ranges; categorical results as counts and percentages. Normality was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test. ROC analysis assessed laboratory measures for predicting GH and estimated AUC, cutoff, sensitivity, and specificity for differentiating GH from NGH. Categorical comparisons used the chi-square test and continuous comparisons used the Kruskal–Wallis test. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Analyses used R software (version 4.0).

document_sections.heading: 3.1 | Patient and Laboratory Characteristics
document_sections.content: Of 703 patients, 371 (52.8%) were female and 332 (47.2%) were male. Median age was 59 years (range, 44–73). dRBC, URD, Cr, eGFR, and ACR differed significantly across the three diagnostic groups; BUN did not differ between glomerular and extrarenal diseases. Glomerular diseases had the highest median dRBC, URD, PCR, and ACR, whereas renal diseases had the highest median BUN and Cr. In Groups 1, 2, and 3, median dRBC (%) was 60, 40, and 5, respectively; median URD (%) was 46.4, 40.1, and 10, respectively. Table 2 provides the demographic and laboratory comparisons. Figure 2 illustrates RBC morphologies classified as dRBC according to Nagahama at ×400.

document_sections.heading: 3.2 | Demographic and RBC Characteristics in the Four Institutions
document_sections.content: Across the four institutions, median dRBC values ranged from 7.0% to 60.0%, and median URD values from 27.2% to 74.1%. Institutional dRBC cutoffs ranged from 5.0 to 67, while URD cutoffs ranged from 25.0% to 35.2%. ROC analysis sought a balance between sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing glomerular from extrarenal disease. The overall AUC was 0.79 for dRBC and 0.83 for URD, without a statistical difference in that comparison. URD had higher sensitivity and specificity than dRBC. Table 3 reports institutional demographics, RBC findings, diagnostic cutoffs, AUCs, sensitivity and specificity, and AUC-comparison p values.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 | Correlation of URD and dRBC Results With Renal Parameters
document_sections.content: Because urine osmolality might affect RBC size, the investigators examined relationships between URD and renal measures. URD correlated significantly with dRBC (0.536), ACR (0.186), BUN (−0.12), and Cr (−0.09), but not with specific gravity (−0.03). dRBC correlated significantly with URD and ACR (0.13). Table 4 presents the broader Spearman correlations among renal-function measures.

document_sections.heading: 3.4 | URD And dRBC Results Among Renal Diseases
document_sections.content: Within renal diseases, patients with acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) had significantly elevated BUN and Cr. Patients with nephrotic syndrome (NS) had significantly elevated dRBC and URD, whereas URD was significantly lower in AKI. Table 5 details the laboratory results and post hoc comparisons across CKD, NS, tubulointerstitial disease, and AKI.

document_sections.heading: 3.5 | Comparison of dRBC and URD Results
document_sections.content: At institution D, dRBC and URD agreed in 78.3% (112/143) of comparisons; 31 findings disagreed. Among eight cases with high URD but low dRBC, small isomorphic RBCs (N = 6) or yeasts (N = 2) might explain the discrepancy. In 23 cases with low URD but high dRBC, dysmorphic cells had normal size, which contributed to the lower URD. Table 6 cross-classifies the two measures and describes discordant morphology. Figure 3 illustrates a case with dRBC of 23.5% and URD of 93.7%, in which predominantly small isomorphic RBCs raised URD; a yeast-interference case with URD of 42.6% despite RBCs being isomorphic (100%); and a case with dRBC of 34% and URD of 1.5%, in which normal-sized dysmorphic RBCs contributed to low URD.

document_sections.heading: 4 | Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors place their findings alongside studies by Charoensappakit, Mizuno, and Cho that evaluated markers other than urinary dRBCs for separating GH from non-GH and reported similar findings. Charoensappakit used FACSCalibur flow cytometry with annexin V-FITC and CD235a-PE to quantify RMPs and PS-exposing RBCs. Although %Total PS-RBCs + RMPs achieved an AUC of 0.9, the authors state that this approach had not entered clinical laboratory use because it cannot measure routine urinalysis parameters such as glucose, albumin, RBC, and WBC and is very costly as a clinical test. Mizuno and Cho used UF-5000 but studied single institutions. Unlike those earlier studies, which grouped diagnoses simply as GH or NGH, the present study reported individual diagnoses across glomerular, renal, and extrarenal categories. The authors report the largest sample and highest URD AUC among these studies: This = 703, Mizuno = 203, and Cho = 263 participants; This = 0.827, Mizuno = 0.649, and Cho = 0.814 for URD AUC between GH and NGH. They also state that only this study compared URD and dRBC distributions within renal disease and investigated causes of discordant findings. Median URD and dRBC were significantly greater in glomerular disease, while BUN and Cr were significantly greater in renal disease than in extrarenal disease. The authors relate this to an earlier study reporting higher small-RBC and lysed-RBC parameters in GH than NGH. URD had an AUC similar to dRBC but better sensitivity and specificity; this study's cutoffs were > 18% for dRBC and > 31.9% for URD. Earlier studies reported clinically significant dRBC cutoffs ranging from 10% to 90%. Median dRBC was low at two participating institutions and high at two, whereas median URD was high at one and similar at the other three. Identifying dRBC in urine sediment requires experience, and variation between observers may account for interlaboratory differences. Instrument-derived URD is easier to obtain, less affected by observer interpretation, and potentially more objective and standardized. A separate study found that > 25% dRBC had high specificity and positive predictive value for glomerular disease or GH and was a significant predictor of GH. Given its comparable AUC and lower between-hospital variability, the authors suggest that URD may be more broadly applicable than dRBC for ruling out non-glomerular causes of hematuria. To investigate whether osmolality affects urinary RBC size, the authors used specific gravity because osmolality had not been measured in every patient. URD was not associated with specific gravity; its correlations with ACR, BUN, and Cr were interpreted as suggesting glomerular damage. Both dRBC and URD were significantly higher in NS, whose principal pathological finding is glomerular damage. CKD and AKI involve varied pathological mechanisms in which glomerular damage may not predominate; URD was significantly lower in AKI. Discordance occurred because normal-sized dRBCs lowered URD or small isomorphic RBCs raised it. Thus, URD and dRBC have similar clinical significance but identify different RBC characteristics. Cho et al. did not examine their correlation; Mizuno et al. reported a coefficient of 0.465, comparable to this study's 0.536. The authors identify variation in dRBC assessments among institutions and the origin of over half the cases at institution K as limitations. They applied the same dRBC guidelines to reduce bias, but ambiguous morphologies prevented consensus because laboratories had to issue patient results. They characterize the use of results as reported by clinical laboratories as reflecting real-world conditions. They believe institution K's predominance did not affect the principal findings of similar URD and dRBC AUCs or the absence of a URD–SG correlation. The authors conclude that comparing serum and urine measures across four hospitals supported their clinical relevance for distinguishing GH from NGH. URD had an AUC comparable to dRBC while being more objective and easier to standardize; they expect it to have broader utility.
